claims.text: The as-synthesized sub-10 nm equiatomic AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles are a metastable single-phase solid solution or highly disordered mixture.
Above 600 K, surface-energy-driven Ostwald ripening overwhelms sluggish diffusion in sub-10 nm AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
Spinodal decomposition begins above 600 K in sub-10 nm AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
The smallest AuCoCuNiPt particles are selectively lost through vaporization or coalescence during heating.
Au and Pt have lower relevant surface energies than Co, Cu, and Ni, creating a surface-energy disparity that drives segregation.
Surface segregation lowers the activation barrier for atomic exchange and diffusion, negating sluggish bulk diffusion.
High surface curvature in sub-10 nm particles creates a substantial chemical-potential gradient above 600 K.
Au and Pt segregate to particle surfaces while Co, Cu, and Ni migrate inward or coalesce.
Elemental segregation reduces the local melting point and increases atomic mobility.
During Ostwald ripening, smaller particles dissolve or evaporate and contribute to the growth of larger phase-separated domains.
Heating to 1000 K will significantly broaden the particle-size distribution and remove particles smaller than 3 nm.
Particles remaining at 1000 K will develop core-shell or multidomain structures with Au/Pt-rich surfaces and Co/Cu/Ni-rich cores.
The average particle size will increase during heating.
High configurational entropy may stabilize solid solutions in equiatomic multielement high-entropy alloys.
High-entropy alloys generally retain a single-phase solid solution up to near-melting temperatures because of sluggish diffusion.
A high-entropy-alloy system can decompose into two phases as a function of composition and annealing temperature.
Surface effects dominate volume effects for AuCoCuNiPt particles smaller than 10 nm.
For bulk AuCoCuNiPt or particles larger than 50 nm, bulk diffusion kinetics and configurational entropy may stabilize a single phase.
The onset temperature for rapid diffusion depends on synthesis-dependent defect density and surface oxide content.
Vacuum pressure may facilitate evaporation of components such as Cu.
